segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Tobin Low, sitting in for Ira Glass. The story of Sara and Ethan's relationship starts with heartbreak. She had just gotten out of a 12-year relationship. He was separated after 13 years of marriage. Neither of them were particularly interested in jumping into something new too fast. But their mutual friends thought, hey, they have that in common. They're both in their 40s, both a little wobbly from their last relationships. They should date. Here's Ethan.

segments.speaker: Ethan
segments.text: I think they saw us both as people who didn't know what they were doing and thought, maybe these two can figure it out together.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: That's both sweet and maybe a little insulting.

segments.speaker: Ethan
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah, I'm going to take it as sweet.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: They hit it off, kept seeing each other, doing date-y stuff-- dinners, museums, walks in the park. And as weeks and then months went by, they advanced to the stage of hanging out with no particular plans. At one point, a kind of big thing happened. A friend of Sarah's died. Ethan knew how hard she was taking it, so he asked her, you want to go to a ball game, take your mind off things? And it felt nice to let him take care of her in that way. It's now been 10 months.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: So you're in contact pretty much every day. You see each other regularly. You're not seeing anybody else. Is he your boyfriend, then?

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Obviously, this is Sara.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: What do you refer to him as?

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: I guess, I use his name.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: And I will often say, he's the person I'm sort of seeing.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: The "sort of" feels crucial there.

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: Or kind of. Or I guess, I'm-- there's always a bit of a qualifier.

segments.speaker: Ethan
segments.text: Gosh. I think both of us have avoided using the boyfriend-girlfriend terms.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: In fact, a couple weeks ago, they had a conversation about whether it was time to have the "what are we" conversation, and they decided to put it off. Ethan and Sara are your classic example of "let's not put a label on it." You know couples like this. And I understand that people do this, but I'm always a little like, why are you doing this dance? If it looks like a boyfriend duck and it quacks like a boyfriend duck, it's just a boyfriend duck, right?

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: Some of my friends will refer to him as my boyfriend. But--

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: You're making a face.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: I'm not very comfortable with it.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Why do you think that is? What does it bring up for you? What is the feeling?

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: It feels like if we put a label on it, gosh, we're going into the tunnel again. It feels like it could last a long time. And that's a little scary. And if I'm someone's girlfriend, I want to be prioritized in a certain way. And I'm going to be reciprocal in that. It's not something that I'm comfortable with right now.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: There are other considerations they're thinking about, like Ethan's daughter, who is 10 and still doesn't really know about Sara. He's thought a lot about what putting a label on this thing with Sara would trigger.

segments.speaker: Ethan
segments.text: If Dad had a girlfriend, I think that that would feel very significant to her. Yeah, I think that that would-- I think it would feel like a big deal to a 10-year-old.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: When I was hearing this described to me at first, I was like-- to be honest, I was like, oh, this sounds very teenager-y, immature. We don't want to call it anything. And now, the more that I've talked to you, it's like, oh, it's a very mature-- and being honest with yourself about what you want and what comes with putting a label on it.

segments.speaker: Sara
segments.text: Oh, yeah. Absolutely. Because there's expectations. And having no expectations is so much nicer right now.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: I get what she's saying. Labels-- they're powerful. They can distill you down to a single word, can get stuck on you without your permission. I still think about the day when my dad introduced me as "his husky boy." I thought about that label for years. Today on our show, we have a story of a woman who spent more than a decade trying to get a particular label put on her. And we see what happens when a label that's holding someone's life together gets peeled away. And also, today, I have the all-powerful label of host, so I am commanding you to stay with us.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: It's This American Life. Act 1, "Last Shift." The label being assigned in this first story is temporary. It's a label that can feel meaningful and definitive. You know the thing will end, whatever it is. But temporary is also a flexible term. Your life on earth is temporary, but it can go on for 100 years.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: The temporary label plays an important role in the US immigration system for something called Temporary Protected Status, TPS. TPS is a status given to a country all at once. It allows eligible people from that country to live and legally work in the US if their home country has become unsafe or unstable, for instance, because of war or disaster. And if war or disaster goes on, TPS can be extended. For some countries, it's been extended for more than 25 years. Wars can last a long time. A 30-second earthquake can cause damage that takes years to recover from.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Last week, the Trump administration succeeded in ending TPS for people from Haiti. A judge removed the last roadblock. It affected a huge number of people, more than 300,000 Haitians. Many have been here in jobs and lives far longer than anyone would consider temporary. So, 300,000 people were facing an end, all at once. Chana Joffe-Walt spent time last week with one of them at her job, a woman named Marie. And no one, including Marie, knew which day would be her very last on the job. Here's Chana.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I had heard about Marie before I showed up at the nursing home in Boston. Her boss told me he was losing his best CNA-- the pride of the building, he said. CNA is a Certified Nursing Assistant. Families love Marie, he told me. When I walked in, the senior nurse leader, Fleurinette, walked me up to the second floor, pointing out details and people along the way. And she pointed to a room and said, the woman staying in this room refused to be moved from her chair to the bed by anyone but Marie.

segments.speaker: Fleurinette
segments.text: If Marie is not here, we have to make sure that we go and tell her why Marie is not here.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Why?

segments.speaker: Fleurinette
segments.text: Because she's used to Marie. She's used to her. And Marie treats her with respect. So she really is an exemplary CNA. I've worked with many CNAs. I know everyone. This is Marie.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oh, hello.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: How are you doing?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I've heard so much about you.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Oh, really?

segments.speaker: Fleurinette
segments.text: Well--

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Oh.

segments.speaker: Fleurinette
segments.text: --this is another Marie.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: A different Marie? OK.

segments.speaker: Fleurinette
segments.text: Yes. This is another Marie.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Apparently, there are a lot of Maries in this building-- Marie Joulet, Marie Claire, Marie France. I ask Fleurinette, how much of the staff here is Haitian? And she says, oh, we all are, except for-- and she scans the floor-- her.

segments.speaker: Fleurinette
segments.text: She is not Haitian. But I think I see three CNAs already, and all three of them are Haitian.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And then, a small woman in glasses, gold hoops, ponytail, and pink scrubs walks purposefully down the hall toward us.

segments.speaker: Fleurinette
segments.text: Chana, here is your Marie.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Nice to meet you.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So nice to meet you. I've heard so much about you already, before even meeting you.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: OK. OK. I'm here a long time.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How long have you been here?

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: 12 years.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Do you know that you have a reputation here as being one of the best?

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Yes, I know. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But Marie is not particularly interested in talking about this or dwelling on her talents. Marie's not a dweller. For a person who's a star, she's the opposite of flashy. She's focused, quiet, exceedingly polite. But I'm asking questions, and I can tell she's distracted, glancing at the rooms behind me, where her residents are.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: I have somebody in the bathroom for now. I'm kind of--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK. So I'll set up. OK, OK.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: OK. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Thanks.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Thank you for coming.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oh, I'm so glad to be here.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: From there, Marie is in motion. And she invites me to follow her, from one resident to the next--

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: I'm coming, mama. I'm coming. I'm coming.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: --in and out of bathrooms and linen closets, between bedsides, humming evangelical hymns to herself, as she changes sheets--

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: [HUMMING]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: --and cleans up messes.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: [WATER RUNNING]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I thought we were going to talk about this huge change that was about to happen in Marie's life, about what is likely her last week on this job. But actually, it seems like I'm going to watch her do her last week on the job. And the other nurses and CNAs are watching me and my microphone and asking each other, what's she doing? She's following Marie? Why? Because she's good at her job? And then they want to talk and add on, saying, I can also tell you how good Marie is at her job.

segments.speaker: Nurse 1
segments.text: She never say no. She always be there for everybody.

segments.speaker: Nurse 2
segments.text: She's just really special.

segments.speaker: Nurse 3
segments.text: She knows all their little quirks. And she'll be training someone and say, they like a sock on their left foot, but not on their right. And she remembers all those things that you don't have to remember to do your job. She's great, so--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And do you know what's happening with Marie this week at the end of this week.

segments.speaker: Nurse 2
segments.text: I do not, no.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK, yeah.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: I get out of the conversation awkwardly and have a couple more moments just like this where I gather, bit by bit, that nobody here knows the major thing that is happening in Marie's life. Marie has invited me here, knowing I'm doing a story about people on TPS, about her job ending. But the people she works with don't know her job is ending, or that she's on TPS, even though most people who work here are Haitian. Some of them are on TPS, like Maria's, but most aren't. A woman on staff named Nancy told me, we give each other privacy.

segments.speaker: Nancy
segments.text: We don't ask questions directly because we don't know who have it, who doesn't have it, and things like that. So we just stay-- talk as a group.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Nancy said the day that the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to end TPS for Haitians, the staff got together at the end of the day and talked about how sad it was that TPS was ending, how scared people were. She said Marie, in particular, was very sympathetic in those conversations toward our other coworkers who have TPS. But Nancy clearly did not know Marie is one of those coworkers.

segments.speaker: Nancy
segments.text: And she was feeling for everybody else. Everybody was talking about it, especially Marie, because she's very caring like that for everybody.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How's it going?

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah?

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: I catch Marie coming out of her room and pull her aside for a minute.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And your coworkers have been asking what I'm doing. And I've been saying, I'm following you. And nobody seems to know about TPS and that stuff. Do you want me not-- I have not said anything.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So you haven't talked to people here about it?

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: No, I don't want to talk to them about it.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK. Can I ask why?

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: I just want--

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: [CHUCKLING]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: If something happened, I cannot come, I will tell them. But for now, nope.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah. If something happens, you would tell them on that day? Is that what you mean?

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: I'm not going to-- after 12 years, I'm not going to just disappear. No, I will tell them. But for now, no, I don't tell them anything. They don't know anything about me.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I learned, the more I talked to more people, that this silence is common. There were so many people on TPS moving through their work days in restaurants, airports, schools, quietly knowing it could end at any moment and not telling anyone. Over 300,000 Haitians on TPS-- that is so many people.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: As immigration statuses go, Temporary Protective Status strikes me as a very strange one. It's not an employment visa, where there can be a path to a more permanent status, like a green card. TPS offers no path. It leads nowhere. You can have it for years. You can have it for decades. It can be terminated at any time.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The executive branch has discretion to offer TPS and discretion to take it away. With other immigration statuses, there's a process. There are steps to take and a system for appeals. TPS is more like a gift from the king, just a thumbs up, thumbs down kind of system.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Haiti is arguably more dangerous than it was in 2011, when Marie was granted TPS. But President Obama was into TPS for Haitians back then, and President Trump today is not. So it's like a vibes-based immigration status. When I asked Marie how she was thinking about TPS, she'd just shrug. What's there to say? What can I do? She told me in Creole, through an interpreter--

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: [SPEAKING CREOLE]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: --I understand the danger that's hanging, but there's nothing else I can do. She doesn't have a lot more to say about that. And maybe there just isn't a lot more to say.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So, how was this going to go, the actual end? For weeks, it was unclear when exactly the TPS termination for Haitians would go into effect. Like, what day? And employers were constantly refreshing government websites and checking the news to try to figure out when to tell their employees they couldn't come back, and how should they do it?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Marie's boss, Colin, told me he was trying to figure out what was the least disruptive, least public way to do this that would protect his employees' privacy. Should he just take them off the schedule, put them on PTO, and tell everyone they're on vacation, and then they just won't come back? Should he do that now? Should he wait?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The deadlines kept changing. TPS was ending on Friday. Then it seemed like maybe it was Monday. But at the end of the day on Monday, I called him, and it seemed like maybe it wasn't Monday.

segments.speaker: Colin
segments.text: I have no idea. I have no idea what's going on right now. I've heard nothing. It feels like, yeah, today is the date, but I'm not getting anything from a government source that says, absolutely, it's the date.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Is there someone to reach out to?

segments.speaker: Colin
segments.text: I can't answer that question without being sarcastic. I mean, I don't know that there is somebody.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Tuesday, I walked into the nursing home at 2:45. I saw Colin on my way into the building, sitting at his desk on the first floor by the entrance-- button-down, large beard. He's 40 years old. I tell Colin I talked to Marie and said I'd be here today for the start of her shift at 3:00. And he said--

segments.speaker: Colin
segments.text: I did meet with HR today. And we have made a company-wide decision that at this point, we are going to take anyone affected by TPS off the schedule. The lack of guidance, we feel like we have to remove them from the schedule.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Wow, OK. So, is she working today?

segments.speaker: Colin
segments.text: She's working today. She's working today.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Does she know that?

segments.speaker: Colin
segments.text: I have not talked to her yet. No. I'm waiting for Marie to come in. I'll let her get settled in. I'll have a conversation with her probably around 4 or 5 o'clock.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How come you wouldn't just tell her when she gets here?

segments.speaker: Colin
segments.text: I don't think it's right to grab somebody walking through the door. Hey, you're walking through the door. So I want to let her settle and have her normal chain. And then I'll sit down and have a conversation with her when we both have time and space to do it. But I do want to have a face-to-face conversation.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Meanwhile, Marie is already here. She's upstairs. She came in through a different door. Her coworkers are greeting her as she sets up.

segments.speaker: Nurse 3
segments.text: Hi, beauty. How are you?

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: I'm OK, baby.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She's in lavender scrubs and a gold and silver headwrap, arranging her cart for her shift. Marie doesn't just grab one of the pre-stocked carts.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: I like to fix my cart. I have to fix it.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You have to do it yourself.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Yeah, yeah. And I put towels, pad, sheet, gown, pillowcase.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: All of a sudden, everything Marie is doing becomes the last time she will do it, counting the blankets and stacking them neatly on the middle shelf. Fitted sheets, diapers, and cream go on the top shelf, pushing her cart to room 101 as the morning shift heads out--

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Nurse 4
segments.text: Bye, Albert. Bye, Marie.

segments.speaker: Nurse 5
segments.text: Bye, Marie. See you tomorrow.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: All right, see you tomorrow. Drive safe home.

segments.speaker: Nurse 5
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: --checking on each resident.

segments.speaker: Resident
segments.text: Hi, Marie.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Hi, how are you?

segments.speaker: Resident
segments.text: I didn't see you yesterday.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: It was my day off.

segments.speaker: Resident
segments.text: Oh?

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Resident
segments.text: I like your silver.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Resident
segments.text: You got to watch out-- the sun.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Resident
segments.text: Put the sunglasses on.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Next door, room 100, is full of visitors. Marie maneuvers quietly around the family, arranging sheets, wiping surfaces, filling water cups. This job is a series of endless small gestures. It's delicate. It's close, difficult work. Marie is both productive and invisible.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: [HUMMING]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She preps the bath and then gently guides the family on how they can be helpful as she washes and changes their 94-year-old mother.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: No, not that.

segments.speaker: Family
segments.text: [INAUDIBLE]

segments.speaker: Mother
segments.text: [INAUDIBLE]

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Mama, Mama.

segments.speaker: Family
segments.text: Mama, tranquila.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Mama, we're just helping you, OK?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Marie is on her way out of room 100, arms full of dirty linens, when Colin enters the hallway to her unit. He walks toward her--

segments.speaker: Colin
segments.text: Hey, Marie.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Yeah. How are you?

segments.speaker: Colin
segments.text: How are you?

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: --but then keeps going. He walks right by her. It looks like he made a last-minute calculation that this is not the time. Marie rolls a cart of soiled linens to the next room, pulls up next to a coworker and whispers to her, asks her where another CNA is today. Marie says, did she call out? That coworker says, yes, I think it's about the TPS thing. They closed it.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Mm-hmm, they closed it. Yes.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Marie says, that's what I heard. Then a call button lights up. She heads toward it, back down the hall.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: You OK? You need to be changed? OK.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Then she's on her way out of that room, and I interrupt. And I ask, have you checked in with Colin?

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: He told me, anything happen, he will call me. He saw me when he came here earlier, but we did not talk.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK. And you haven't asked? You haven't asked him anything?

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: No, no, no. I don't want to embarrass him.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Why would it be embarrassing for him?

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Because he doesn't like me to leave.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: He doesn't want you to leave?

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Yeah. He's not happy to see me leave. I'm not going to ask him anything.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Next to us, a man in the hallway with bright yellow socks has been using his long legs to drag his wheelchair back and forth, saying, I don't know, I don't know, I don't know. And a nurse leans close to Marie and says, could you help my friend with the catheter?

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: For the catheter?

segments.speaker: Nurse 7
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Yeah. Come. Come, papa.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Colin comes by again, glances in the rooms, but Marie is in the bathroom.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Oh, oh, pull the pants down. [HUMMING]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She empties the catheter.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: [LIQUID SPLASHING]

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: [HUMMING]

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: [WATER RUNNING]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: As this is happening, Colin does a lap. Marie pushes the man back into the hallway, and Colin spots her coming out of the room, but the man with the yellow socks is agitated and pointing at his pants. He wants Marie to change his pants, too.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Like this. No.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Oh, you want, too, another pants? Come. [HUMMING]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So they're back into the room.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: OK, stand up, papa.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [GROANING]

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Take your time. No, no. Don't slide.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: [GROANS]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Colin disappears back downstairs.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How do you end a 12-year career without interrupting, without disruption, without anyone noticing? Colin is looking for an opening to do this quietly, but there is not one. This is a person who is busy and needed. CNAs are hard to find and hard to keep all over the country. The average time people stay in these jobs is two years.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And here's Marie. Her boss doesn't want her to leave. And she doesn't want to leave. He doesn't want to embarrass her. And she doesn't want to embarrass him. This is not the version of removing people that we've seen so much of in the last year and a half. It's not people grabbed in public, pulled out of cars in dramatic, sometimes violent, videos. This is a silent play being performed in workplaces across the country, the quietest ending everyone involved can possibly pull off.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: By 5:30 PM, when the dinner trays arrive, Marie is moving between residents, arranging bedside tables, delivering food trays. A visitor tells her, we're going to head out now. My grandma's alone. Keep an eye.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: You're leaving?

segments.speaker: Visitor
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: She's OK.

segments.speaker: Visitor
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Visitor
segments.text: She'll be here by herself.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Visitor
segments.text: All right. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: OK, no problem. I will take care.

segments.speaker: Visitor
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Marie
segments.text: OK, bye.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Marie reassures her, then spots a man who's come to have dinner with his wife. Marie finds a folding chair, places it behind him without saying anything, and keeps walking. Meanwhile, Colin is on the second floor now, and he's not leaving. I can hear him faintly somewhere on the other side of the nurses' station, talking to some guy about printers, I think.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: At 6:00 PM, Colin just walks straight to Marie's unit and scans the area. He sees her carrying empty dinner trays. He says quietly, hey, Marie, you got a minute? Sure, she says. She places the trays down and follows him down the hall. They go into a room with an interpreter. It takes seven minutes. Colin doesn't want me to record. And when Marie comes out, I don't turn the recorder back on.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She says to me, well, they're taking me off the schedule for now, until he has more information. This is maybe the end. I tell her I'm sorry. She says, they said I can go home now or finish my shift. It's up to me. I have the choice. And then Marie does something I have not yet seen her do. She talks about how good she is at this job. She says, when I started here in 2014, my salary was very low. Every year, they saw the way I'm working and the work I've done. And every year, they gave me more. Right now, I won't tell you how much I make, but it's double where I started.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I tell her, I'm sure you deserve it. She gets choked up and says, thank you. Then, she says, she's decided to finish her shift, and she should get back to it. She stands up and walks back down the hall.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Chana Joffe-Walt is a producer on our show. Coming up, a comedian walks into a bar and walks out with a medical mystery. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio, when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Tobin Low, sitting in for Ira Glass. Today's show, "Label Maker!" a show all about the power of labels. We're at Act Two of our show. Act 2, "Diagnose Me, Maybe."

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: So the whole reason I've been thinking about labels lately is because of this next story we're doing today. It's about Janet McNamara, a very funny comedian who had this odd thing happen to her 15 years ago when she was first getting started. What happened was, this one night, she's performing at a comedy club in Boston, where she's proudly from-- I think all Irish Catholics are. Anyway, she gets off stage, goes to the green room, when the owner of the club stops her.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: He just kind of said, out of curiosity, what's that thing when you look up in the air, and you dart your eyes? And I do this thing. I have really bad memory recall. So I look up in the air a lot when I can't think of a word or I can't think of what I'm going to say next. And I said, that's what I do when I'm thinking. And he said, have you ever been tested for autism? And I said, no, I've never considered that I'm autistic before. Literally, nobody has ever said it to me before.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: And where was this comedy club?

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: It was called Dick Doherty's Comedy Vault. And this guy, Dick Doherty, he's the first person who asked me if I was autistic.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Oh, it was the namesake of the club.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: Yeah. He named a club after himself. Yes, correct.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Gotcha.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Janet brushed it off, thought it was sort of funny. And she is a comedian, so she started getting on stage around Boston, telling the story about this guy asking this question out of nowhere. It got laughs. But also, after the show, people would come up to her and say, hey--

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: I'm autistic. Just to let you know, you're also autistic.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: They'd say it that bluntly?

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: And how would that feel? How would you react?

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: I would say, I don't think I am.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Janet says, as a kid growing up in the '90s, she'd been tested many times for learning disabilities, for anxiety. Never once did any of those medical professionals say the word "autistic." When she talked about it with her family, her friends, they'd say, yeah, it's a little weird that you get your hair cut in slow increments, so no one says, hey, you got a haircut. But mainly, they said--

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: You're not autistic. You're from Boston.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: But the fact that people kept saying it to her after shows, it raised a curiosity. She thought, it's probably nothing, but what's the harm in asking my psychiatrist if he thinks it's possible? Here's Janet talking on stage about what this all led to.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: It was when Asperger's was still a thing. It's not a thing anymore. Now, they call it the autism spectrum. They unnamed it. He was a Nazi. Asperger's was a Nazi. Yeah, read a book.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: I remember I took the test, and the guy, he just looked up from his notebook and he goes, well, people with Asperger's generally have above average IQs, so--

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: I'm not smart enough to be mildly autistic--

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: --is what that doctor told me.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: This, again, was her actual psychiatrist. Janet decided to let it go, partly because this was back in the 2010s. And the idea of an adult getting tested for autism, it just wasn't in the air the same way it is now. She thought, OK, that's it. No need to keep pushing for a test. So for years, autism was just a funny bit on stage, part of her standup. But offstage, Janet had a day job. And what was happening there would turn out to be not so funny.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Offstage, Janet had found what she thought was the perfect job. She was an accountant, worked her way into it after being a bookkeeper for a plumbing company right out of college. She liked accounting because she was essentially a problem-solver. Looked at ledgers, Excel spreadsheets, pointed out where there were errors. And her boss loved her because Janet got her job done quickly and efficiently-- no small talk, no bullshit.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: She even got raises regularly. That is, until one day, she got a new boss, one who liked small talk, wanted more group meetings, more socializing amongst coworkers. Early on, this new boss asked Janet to meet one-on-one so they could get to know each other.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: And she said, I have two kids. I enjoy hiking. And then she turned around and showed me her two kids with a-- she showed me a-- she turned around and picked up a framed picture of her two kids and went to hand it to me. And I just said, I could see that from here. When I walked into her office, I saw the pictures of her kids. I immediately knew, when I walked into her office, she has two kids. They're about 12 years old. The boy's older than the girl. OK, cool. I know all this information.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Clocked. I know this. I got it.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: And then she just tells me verbally and then hands me the picture, and I'm like, I already know this. Why are we talking about this? You have a picture. That's why you have a picture on your desk, is so that people don't start asking if you have kids because there's a picture on your desk.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Janet talks in her act about how things started to sour for her in the workplace.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: I was having a hard time at work at the time. I was having a hard time at work because of my personality.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: Yeah, they said I was rude at work. They said I had bad tone. They said I had bad tone in my emails. I was like, how could you have bad tone in an email? I wasn't singing.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: I was like, you people need to relax. I told my boss to relax during a performance improvement plan.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: And even though she joked about it on stage, it was serious. Seemed like she might lose her job. And what made it so difficult was that it felt like she wasn't being asked to improve her work. She was always good at that part. It was like she was being asked to change her personality, her fundamental way of being, which, how do you even go about fixing that?

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: She became so anxious and stressed about it. She took medical leave for a while, hoping she could figure out a solution. And then she went to talk to a doctor about what that might look like, like a more private desk away from the chatter of the office, the ability to sit out those meetings with large groups of people. She asked the doctor if he could help her ask for these accommodations. And he said, those sound like what you'd ask for if you were autistic-- again, that label. Janet decided to look into a diagnosis again, this time because the need had become dire.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Janet goes for her first official autism test, which, this time, was an actual real deal test. Testing for autism, by the way, is complex because there's no blood test. Instead, there are usually multiple sessions during which the tester is looking at social interactions, sensory issues, repetitive behaviors, or fixated interests. And then they take all of this into account to assign a diagnosis, which is what Janet went through this time.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: I don't know if anybody's ever had one. It's like this whole thing. It's like a three-day thing. You look at pictures of people, and they're like, they look happy, they look sad. And they send surveys. And I was perfect. I had everything perfect, and I didn't get the diagnosis. Like I said, I didn't get it. And he knew I wanted it, too.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: I didn't get it. And I'll tell you what happens. At the end of the day, the guy, he just came back, and he just looked at me right in the eye, which I did not care for.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: I swear, he just looks at me right in the eye, and he goes, you are so close.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: I swear to god, he goes, you're so close. You just didn't quite hit all the criteria. And the criteria I didn't hit, the only reason why I'm not autistic, according to him, is because the tags on my shirts don't bother me. Yeah, I don't have sensory issues. I was pissed. I was all ready to go back to work and be like, hey, I don't have to look at you. It's not that I'm rude. It's that I don't understand. It turns out I'm just rude.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: You could tell that I'm rude because the tags on my shirts don't bother me. And that's the difference between rude and autistic.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: It definitely felt-- it felt like I had no choice but to change. And it felt like I had no choice but to start playing the game, which is talking about the weather and saying hi to people. And I did start learning people's kids names.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: How long do you feel like you were able to keep that up at that job specifically?

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: Oh, like three months. My brain just wasn't-- it's so hard to describe. It's probably what dementia feels like, in that you know this isn't hard, but your brain just can't do it. I just couldn't function.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Janet cycled through several corporate jobs after that. She said she'd do well, but then hit a wall, as the demands of interacting and socializing would increase. She'd have to quit or face being fired.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: That's the cycle Janet's been in for the last decade, trying to avoid situations in everyday life that would make her uncomfortable, but then when they do happen, talking about them on stage for laughs and how she still can't get a fucking diagnosis. So she's just kind of been toughing it out, until recently, when she had an experience that flipped her thinking about everything. She took a kid to the movies, kid she was babysitting, a kid she knew well. And at the movies, this kid started to cuddle with her, as little kids do.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: And it was so uncomfortable to me that she was stroking my arm. But I also understood that it was a little kid and that you can't just tell a little kid to-- I understood that it was, like, her way of showing affection. And I just felt so stuck. And I started crying.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Because you had to deal with it. It was your problem to deal with.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: I felt like I'm the adult. I just need to take this.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Janet went from discomfort to just being flat-out mad at herself.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: [SNIFFLING] How awful are you as a person if you just want to say to a little kid, like, stop touching me. Stop cuddling with me. Stop showing me affection. It just doesn't feel good on a human level as a person to not want to cuddle with a little kid, and for that to be an overwhelming experience.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: She told all this to her current therapist, and her therapist said to her, I think we should revisit getting a diagnosis. I think it's right for you, and the other testers got it wrong. Janet was ready to stop blaming herself, so she agreed.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: It was very much a, maybe there's nothing wrong with me. Maybe my brain is just wired different. And maybe I need to not beat myself up.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: And that's when I interviewed Janet, when she was trying yet again to get a diagnosis. When I talked to her, it was right before she was about to find out her results. When they did finally come in, she was standing outside a bar. It was 11:00 PM. She opened an email with a report. And then, the next night, she went on stage in Portland, Maine, and dropped the news.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: And the lady was like, I don't know what's going on, but you're definitely autistic.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: [LAUGHTER, CHEERING]

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: She was like, you're autistic because you are interested in people. And you're just not interested in things that are boring. And you're not interested in boring people who don't do puzzles correctly.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: [CHEERING]

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: And she said I have a rigid personality. I'm rigid. And I said, I'm not rigid. I'm just, most of the time, right.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: And we talked about how my least favorite thing my therapist says is sometimes my therapist will be like, hey, two things can be true. And I'll be like, yeah, I agree, two things could be true. But in this case, one thing is true.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: The next time I see her, she tells me she's pretty stoked about it, but not for the reason I thought. She tells me about a recent experience interacting with a woman in a class she's taking.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: I sit in a specific seat every day. And I walked in, and she was sitting in my seat. And she said to me, I'm sitting in your seat. Do you want me to move? And I said, no, it's OK. I'll sit over here. And she was like, are you sure? And we had this back and forth. And I actually said, actually, I really want to sit in that seat. Can you move? And she moved. And she wasn't upset at all. She was perfectly fine with it.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: And I've just never felt that seen before, where somebody's sitting in my seat, they saw my face, they saw that I was distressed. They didn't see it as a control thing or like I'm taking it-- they didn't take it personally that I was like, you're in my seat. It felt very good. Yeah, and there's no way she knew I was autistic. There was just something about the way I approached it, which is that I understood.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: I think six months ago, I would have said, she's an asshole. She's sitting in my seat. What's wrong with her? Why would she sit in my seat? I would have taken it personally, like she was fucking with me, or she was messing with me by sitting in my seat, as opposed to knowing that it's something that I'm specifically sensitive about, that I want to sit in the same place. So, yeah.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: It seems like it brings up a lot of emotion for you, where it's--

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: Yeah, it's weird. It's like a different way of feeling seen, even without telling people about the diagnosis. And there's something different. I don't know exactly how I'm approaching people differently that they're not taking it personally that their behavior is affecting me. It's great. I had no idea that it would be so different. And I didn't realize that you don't even have to tell people. The way I'm approaching people is different.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: It's true. When we sat down for this last interview, we were waiting for the studio to be set up, and she said, I'm fine if we don't make small talk while we wait, pretty matter-of-factly. And I understood. So we sat there in a very comfortable silence.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Janet McNamara is a comedian. You can watch her full special, Not Smart Enough, on YouTube.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Act 3, "The Last Description." When you get down to it, labels are just our way of pointing out what we think is remarkable about other people. That's writer Alfred Jung Lee's argument. He's been thinking a lot about what we notice in each other, especially as he tries to describe someone very close to him. Here's Alfred.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: (HOST) ALFRED LEE JUNG: Not long ago, I was reading in a magazine profile a description of a person who, quote, "has a prodigious white beard, wavy gray bangs, and dark beetling eyebrows." A photo of the person was included. And as I looked, I admired the efficiency of the description. It did not say that the man had two arms and a nose. These details were assumed.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: Reflecting on this, it occurred to me that when one describes a person, one is also describing how that person deviates from the norm, what makes them different from everyone else. Recently, someone I'd never met was supposed to pick me up from an airport in the Midwest, and I offered a succinct description of myself-- Asian guy with too much luggage, I texted.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: I walked out of the airport, towing two suitcases, a carry-on, and a backpack. I heard a stranger shout my name. I was recognized before I'd even made it to the curb. Description draws attention to what is different about a thing. "Asian guy with too much luggage" is a good description in Cedar Rapids, less so in Seoul. The greater the focus on what is most different, the better the description.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: In an online support group I attended for spousal loss, people often described their dead spouses. The descriptions usually followed a formula. The points of variation included their job. The dead spouse was an accountant, a store manager, a health care worker. In personality, they were "stubborn" or "loved to joke." There was a woman who had liked motorcycles, a man who had been a tender father to kids who were not biologically his own. Sometimes we shared pictures.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: Even as I looked at the pictures and listened to the descriptions, I found it hard to understand that they were once alive. When someone described their spouse as "stubborn," I took it to mean their spouse had been more stubborn than the average person. But I wasn't sure what this really said. Most of a description goes unsaid.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: Lately, my reality has transformed without my noticing, and I have been struggling to describe it. My father called me the other day from Korea, and it gave me a chance to try. I described the weather in my new hometown in the Midwest, the one where I'd been picked up at the airport, saying that it was in the 70s at the moment, late in the afternoon, that I was 10 minutes from campus, where I decided to go back to school for a writing program, and that the city was hilly and not flat.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: He asked about my new friends and classmates, and I told him what I've been telling everyone-- mid 20s to late 30s, everyone seemingly smart and nice. I told him about my studio apartment, that there was enough room, that it got good light, about the places I could walk to from the apartment.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: But there was something else hovering over our conversation, another picture that was not being described. It was what my life would have looked like if things had gone according to plan, and how this current situation, far from anywhere I had ever imagined, may or may not have differed from that plan, which might also inform whether or not I was doing OK, and, therefore, whether or not my father needed to worry. It was this second picture, this other life that we were talking around, and the extent to which my present life may or may not have varied from it that our conversation was also about.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: I remember one time when I felt I understood something about one of the other dead spouses. Instead of her spouse, a woman described an electric razor. It had belonged to her husband, and he had used it on many mornings. She used to hate the noise, but now that he was dead, she missed the sound of the stupid thing when she woke up. Somehow, he came alive to me then, though this detail was routine and did not distinguish him. She held the razor in her hand and flipped it on for us.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: People want to know what she looked like. Children especially want to see pictures. But in the last five years of her life, my wife's most noticeable characteristics were often related to either cancer or treatment. She lost and regrew her hair more than once and sometimes wore a rotation of wigs, none of which quite suited her. She gained and lost large amounts of weight, and over time, her face swelled. When one looks at a picture of her from these years, one often sees a sick person before anything else, while at other times, one sees someone vibrant and healthy. I am not sure which version to describe.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: More variables-- she was 28 when she was diagnosed with stage IV cancer, 33 when she died. Her driver's license says she was 5 foot 6 and 115 pounds, with brown hair and green eyes-- although the weight was incorrect, perhaps one of those things she had filled out as a teenager and carried over for years. It became correct again as she sickened and then dropped well below that number.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: In my memory, her eyes are more brown than the green that was documented. I could say that when she was healthy, her hair was thin, often not much longer than shoulder length, sometimes worn with a headband and usually not long enough to tie up, although I can't even be sure about this last part without checking photographs. When she was young, her dad used to tease her about having a big head. Sometimes I offer that she was white, but usually, I wait until the question is asked. Sometimes I envy the white person with a dead spouse, of whom the question would be less likely to be asked.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: In her eulogy, I described the thing about her that I found most distinctive-- the way the air around her would transform and still and her entire body react when she felt something deeply, whether she was encountering a view of the ocean, the dye of a fabric, a memory. In these moments, she might whisper or cry. And I felt that if I touched her skin, she would dissolve into vapor.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: In those moments, I could also see the young child who had been too sensitive to the world. In family lore, she had been a problem child, emotional and inconsolable, prone to tantrums. A sense of injustice followed her throughout her life and still got the better of her sometimes. Perhaps for this reason, she was a quick and firm judge of character. She gave me a list of people she did not want at her memorial.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: I can also describe those less obvious distinctions that reveal themselves only after long periods of attention, that she tilted her head slightly as a greeting when she walked toward someone she knew, that in her sleep, she raised her arms into the air and slowly scratched one and then the other, that she became nervous and reached for my hand when an airplane was about to take off.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: Yet, increasingly, these details feel irrelevant. As time passes, she becomes more to me, the things that made her just like other people. I think of two arms and two ears and a nose that sometimes ran. She owned socks and scarves, wrapped a towel around herself after a shower, wrote cards, rode the bus, walked around puddles, opened and closed curtains, listened and asked questions, got hungry and tired, sometimes wore sneakers. She was like anyone else, which is to say that simply by breathing, she created life and atmosphere.

segments.speaker: Alfred Lee Jung
segments.text: This increasingly seems to me the point, the description of the thing itself, rather than what makes it different. I will try to describe one of the happiest days of my life. My partner and I are leaving the hospital. She has been through her first year of surgery, recovery, drug treatment. She holds in her hand the printout of a radiology report. It describes scanned images of her body, of her head, chest, abdomen, pelvis. The report for each of the four scans gives the following descriptions-- unremarkable, unremarkable, unremarkable, unremarkable. On this day, there is nothing about her worth describing.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Alfred Jung Lee is a writer in Iowa City. This essay was originally published in The Believer. Our version was produced by Diane Wu.

The people who put today's show together include Phia Bennin, Dana Chivvis, Emmanuel Dzotsi, Cassie Howley, Adriene Lilly, Seth Lind, Molly Marcello, Andrea Marks, Katherine Rae Mondo, Stowe Nelson, Nadia Reiman, Anthony Roman, Ryan Rumery, Ruby Schwartz, Alissa Shipp, Christopher Swetala.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Our managing editor is Sarah Abdurrahman. Our senior editors, David Kestenbaum and Nancy Updike. Special thanks this week to Betsy Johnson, Allan Phillips, Lindsay Naeder, and Marta Chmielowicz at Autism Speaks, Kory Andreas, Se Eun Gong, Leading Age, Melissa Honig, Evelyn Marte, Amina Dubuisson, Yves Vilas, and the other workers on TPS who shared their experiences with us.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: Thanks, also, to all of our This American Life Partners. Their support is an essential part of our budget. Subscribe as a Life Partner, and you'll get regular, exclusive bonus episodes. You'll listen ad-free. And you'll help us continue to make the show. Join at thisamericanlife.org/lifepartners. That link is also in the show notes.

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: This American Life is delivered to public radio stations by PRX, the Public Radio Exchange. Thanks, as always, to my boss, Ira Glass. He's off this week, working on his new radio show, That American Life. He says our show is old news.

segments.speaker: Janet McNamara
segments.text: I'm like, I already know this. Why are we talking about this?

segments.speaker: Tobin Low
segments.text: I'm Tobin Low. Ira Glass will be back next week with more stories of This American Life.
